s: この奨学金は国籍（　　）、日本の大学に在籍する留学生ならだれでも申し込める。
en: This scholarship is open to any international student enrolled at a Japanese university, regardless of nationality.
why: 〜を問わず takes a word with a range of values (国籍, 年齢) and says the same rule covers all of them. Typical of official notices.
〜にもかかわらず means 'even though'. It needs a fact that should have blocked the result. 国籍 is a range, not a fact.
〜もかまわず criticises a person for ignoring something they should mind. A scholarship rule is not someone's careless behaviour.
〜はさておき drops a topic in conversation to move to the main point. It cannot say who is eligible.
tell: A range word (国籍, 年齢) + 'anyone can' in a rule: を問わず.

s: このコールセンターでは、昼夜（　　）専門のスタッフが電話での相談を受け付けている。
en: At this call centre, specialist staff take phone enquiries day and night.
why: 〜を問わず takes an opposing pair like 昼夜 or 男女 and covers both sides. 昼夜を問わず is the fixed way to say 'around the clock'.
〜にもかかわらず needs a fact that should have stopped the result, like 深夜にもかかわらず. A pair like 昼夜 is not a fact.
〜はともかく parks something less important to stress something else. Nothing is parked here: the point is that both day and night are covered.
〜をめぐって means 'over' a dispute or debate. Nobody is arguing about day and night.
tell: An opposing pair (昼夜, 男女, 有無) with no も: を問わず.

s: この大会は天候（　　）実施しますので、各自雨具をご用意ください。
en: This event will be held whatever the weather, so please bring your own rain gear.
why: 〜を問わず takes a word with a range (天候: sun, rain, wind) and says the plan holds for all of it. The organiser's plan (実施します) can follow.
〜にもかかわらず needs a fact that has happened, like 悪天候. It also bans the speaker's plan after it, and 実施します is the organiser's plan.
〜もかまわず describes someone carelessly ignoring what they should mind. It also bans the speaker's own intention after it.
〜どころか needs two things far apart on one scale (far from A, even B). 天候 and holding the event are not on one scale.
tell: A range word + the organiser's plan: を問わず. にもかかわらず needs a fact and bans plans after it.

s: どのような事情があるか（　　）、無断欠勤は認められません。
en: Whatever your circumstances, absence without notice is not permitted.
why: 〜にかかわらず can take a question-word clause (どのような〜か, どちらを選ぶか): whatever the answer, the result is the same.
〜にもかかわらず has も and means 'even though'. It needs a settled fact, not an open question like どのような事情があるか.
〜もかまわず describes someone carelessly ignoring what they should mind. This sentence states a rule, not a person's behaviour.
〜に応じて means the result changes to match the variable. Here the result never changes: absence is not allowed.
cue: どのような事情があるか
tell: Question word + か, and the result never changes: にかかわらず. No も.

s: 商品をお買い上げになる、ならない（　　）、ご試着はご自由にどうぞ。
en: Whether or not you buy anything, you are welcome to try items on.
why: 〜にかかわらず takes a yes or no pair (なる・ならない, 行く・行かない): either way, the offer stands.
〜にもかかわらず needs a settled fact and bans invitations and requests after it. ご自由にどうぞ is an invitation.
〜もかまわず criticises someone's careless act. It also bans invitations and requests after it.
〜に限らず means 'not only X, but wider too' (子どもに限らず大人も). A yes or no pair is not something you can widen.
cue: お買い上げになる、ならない
tell: A yes or no verb pair (する・しない) + an invitation or request: にかかわらず.

s: 屋外コンサートは、当日（　　）予定どおり開催します。
en: The outdoor concert will go ahead as planned, whether or not it rains on the day.
c: 雨が降るかどうかにかかわらず
雨が降ったにもかかわらず
雨が降るかどうかもかまわず
why: 〜かどうかにかかわらず: rain or no rain, the plan stays the same. It fits a future event and the organiser's plan.
〜にもかかわらず needs a fact that has already happened. The concert is still ahead, and the organiser's plan (開催します) cannot follow it.
〜もかまわず criticises someone's careless behaviour and bans the speaker's intention after it. 開催します is the organiser's intention.
〜(よ)うものなら warns that a disaster would follow. 'Held as planned' is not a disaster.
cue: 予定どおり開催します
tell: Future event, either way, organiser's plan: かどうかにかかわらず. にもかかわらず needs a past fact.

s: 彼は周りの人が迷惑そうな顔をしている（　　）、電車の中で大声で電話を続けた。
en: Without caring that the people around him looked annoyed, he kept talking loudly on the phone on the train.
why: 普通形 + の + もかまわず: someone acts without minding what a normal person would mind. The speaker's criticism of him is built in.
〜を問わず takes a range word or a pair (年齢, 男女). A whole clause about people looking annoyed is neither.
〜はともかく parks X to stress something that matters more (X はともかく、Y は〜). No second, more important point follows here; there is only what he did.
〜どころか contrasts two things far apart on one scale (far from A, even B). Looking annoyed and phoning loudly are not on one scale.
cue: 迷惑そうな顔をしている
tell: Someone ignores what they should mind (others' annoyance, being seen): のもかまわず.

s: 母は自分の服が汚れる（　　）、泥だらけの子犬を抱き上げた。
en: Without caring that her own clothes would get dirty, my mother picked up the muddy puppy.
why: 普通形 + の + もかまわず: someone acts without minding what most people would mind (dirty clothes). It describes another person's behaviour, here with admiration rather than criticism.
〜はさておき is the speaker dropping a topic to get to the main one. It cannot describe what another person ignored.
〜をめぐって means 'over' a dispute. Nobody is arguing about dirty clothes.
〜どころか says the opposite of X is true (far from X). But her clothes did get dirty; that is the point of the sentence.
tell: Someone else acts without minding a cost most people would mind (dirt, being seen): のもかまわず.

s: 実際に役に立つかどうか（　　）、一度試してみる価値はあると思う。
en: Whether or not it actually turns out to be useful, I think it's worth trying once.
why: 〜はともかく parks a question for now (〜かどうか is fine before it) because what follows matters more: it is worth a try.
〜にもかかわらず needs a settled fact. 〜かどうか is still open, so it cannot come before にもかかわらず.
〜もかまわず criticises someone for ignoring what they should mind. Here the speaker gives an opinion, not a report of careless behaviour.
〜をめぐって means 'over' a dispute and needs a debate or conflict after it. The sentence ends in a calm opinion.
tell: Park an open question (〜かどうか) and stress what matters more: はともかく.

s: この掃除機は、デザイン（　　）、吸い込む力の強さは他社の製品よりずっと上だ。
en: Its design aside, this vacuum cleaner has far stronger suction than other makers' products.
why: 〜はともかく sets X aside as less important, then praises what matters more (the suction). Typical shape: X はともかく、Y は〜.
〜を問わず needs a range or a pair (年齢, 男女). One product has one design, so there is no range here.
〜もかまわず describes a person ignoring something they should mind. A vacuum cleaner does not act.
〜どころか contrasts two points on one scale (far from A, even B). Design and suction are different scales.
tell: X aside, Y is what counts (X はともかく、Y は + praise): はともかく.

s: 堅い話（　　）、まずは乾杯しましょう。
en: Serious talk aside, let's start with a toast.
why: 〜はさておき drops a topic for now and moves on to what comes first. An invitation like 〜ましょう can follow.
〜を問わず needs a range or a pair (年齢, 男女). 堅い話 has neither.
〜もかまわず criticises careless behaviour, and an invitation (〜ましょう) cannot follow it.
〜にかかわらず needs a range, a pair or 疑問詞〜か. 堅い話 is a single topic, not a range.
tell: Drop the topic for now and do this first (〜ましょう): はさておき.

s: A「昨日の試合、最後まで見ました？すごかったですね。」B「ええ、本当に。それ（　　）、例の報告書はもう出しましたか。」
en: A: 'Did you watch yesterday's match to the end? It was amazing.' B: 'Yes, it really was. That aside, have you handed in that report yet?'
why: それはさておき closes the topic just discussed (the match) and moves to the real business (the report).
それどころか means 'far from it, in fact even more'. It needs a stronger statement on the same line, not a new question.
それにもかかわらず means 'even so' and needs a result that defies the last fact. B is changing the subject, not reporting a result.
〜を問わず needs a range or a pair (年齢, 男女). それ, the chat about the match, is neither.
tell: Close the chat you were having and switch to business: それはさておき.

s: 一度も授業に出ていない彼が、試験で満点を取れる（　　）。
en: There's no way he could get full marks on the exam when he hasn't attended a single class.
why: 〜わけがない is total denial: the speaker is certain it cannot happen. Not one class attended makes full marks unthinkable.
〜わけではない is partial denial ('not necessarily', 'not entirely'). The context calls for certainty, not a hedge.
〜というものでもない denies a general rule of thumb, often after 〜ば. This is about one specific student.
〜わけにはいかない means 'I can't very well' for social reasons and needs a deliberate action. 取れる is a potential verb, and nothing social blocks a good score.
cue: 一度も授業に出ていない
tell: An outcome the facts make unthinkable, said with certainty: わけがない (total denial).

s: あんなに口の堅い山田さんが、会議の内容を外部の人に漏らす（　　）。何かの誤解だろう。
en: There's no way Yamada, who is so discreet, would leak what was said in the meeting to outsiders. It must be some misunderstanding.
why: 〜わけがない: total denial. Knowing how discreet Yamada is, the speaker is sure he did not leak it, so it must be a misunderstanding.
〜わけではない only denies part of something ('not entirely'). The speaker is not hedging; he rejects the idea completely.
〜わけにはいかない is about the speaker's own social limits (I can't very well). It cannot judge whether someone else did something.
〜わけだ means 'so it follows'. It would accept that he leaked it, which clashes with 何かの誤解だろう.
cue: あんなに口の堅い山田さんが
tell: あんな〜な人が + an act out of character + certainty: わけがない.

s: どんなに優秀でも、入社したばかりの新人がこんな大きな取引を一人で（　　）。
en: However talented they are, there's no way a brand-new hire could close a deal this big on their own.
c: まとめられるわけがない
まとめられないわけではない
まとめさせるわけにはいかない
why: 可能形 + わけがない: however talented, a newcomer simply cannot do it. どんなに〜でも sets up exactly this kind of total denial.
〜ないわけではない says 'it is not impossible'. That clashes with どんなに優秀でも, which means talent would not change the answer.
The subject is 新人が, so the causative まとめさせる does not fit. 〜わけにはいかない is also about the speaker's own social limits.
〜わけだ means 'so it follows that they can'. That contradicts どんなに優秀でも.
cue: 入社したばかりの新人が
tell: どんなに〜でも + clearly impossible: 〜られるわけがない.

s: 薬を飲んだのに、熱は下がる（　　）、かえって上がってしまった。
en: Even though I took medicine, far from going down, my fever actually went up.
why: 〜どころか: reality is the opposite of A. かえって ('on the contrary') is the giveaway.
〜ばかりか adds something in the same direction ('not only A, but also B'). 下がる and 上がる point in opposite directions.
〜上に also stacks two things in the same direction. It cannot link opposites.
〜ものか is an angry denial at the end of a sentence. It cannot link two clauses.
tell: Far from A, the opposite happened (かえって, 逆に): どころか.

s: 生活がかなり苦しいらしく、彼には貯金（　　）、友人からの借金が百万円以上もあるそうだ。
en: He's apparently struggling to get by: far from having savings, he owes friends over a million yen.
why: 〜どころか: far from A (savings), the opposite B (debt). 生活がかなり苦しい tells you he has no savings.
〜ばかりか means 'not only A but also B', so he would have savings too. That clashes with 生活がかなり苦しい.
〜はもとより means 'A, of course, and also B'. It also says he has savings, which the first clause rules out.
〜に限らず means 'not limited to A'. It still assumes he has savings, so it clashes with 生活がかなり苦しい.
cue: 生活がかなり苦しいらしく
tell: Far from A, the opposite B (savings → debt): どころか. ばかりか only adds in the same direction.

s: A「駅前の新しいラーメン屋、はやると思う？」B「店員があんなに失礼なんだから、客が集まる（　　）。」
en: A: 'Do you think the new ramen shop by the station will catch on?' B: 'With staff that rude? As if customers would ever flock there!'
why: 〜ものか: a heated, spoken 'as if!'. B denies the idea completely, with feeling. Casual speech fits it.
〜わけではない is a soft, partial denial ('not entirely'). B is not hedging; he rejects the idea outright.
〜というものではない denies a general rule, often after 〜ば. B is judging one shop, not stating a rule.
〜ものなら means 'if only I could' and needs a potential verb and a wish after it. It cannot end the sentence.
cue: あんなに失礼なんだから
tell: Casual, heated total denial of a fact: 〜ものか (〜もんか).

s: 母「あの子が自分から部屋を（　　）。いつも私が言わないと何もしないんだから。」
en: Mother: 'As if that child would ever tidy his room on his own! He never does a thing unless I tell him.'
c: 片付けるものですから
片付けられるものなら
why: 〜ものですか is the polite spoken form of 〜ものか: 'as if he would!'. Often used by women, it fits the mother's irritation.
〜ものですから gives an excuse ('it's just that he tidies'). The next sentence says he never does, so it contradicts.
た形 + ものです looks back fondly on a past habit ('he used to tidy'). The next sentence is about what he always does now.
〜ものなら needs a wish or a dare after it in the same sentence. It cannot end with a full stop.
cue: いつも私が言わないと何もしない
tell: An annoyed 'as if!' about someone else's behaviour: 〜ものですか, not 〜ものですから.

s: 日本に長く住んでいるからといって、必ずしも敬語が完璧に使える（　　）。
en: Just because someone has lived in Japan a long time doesn't necessarily mean they can use keigo perfectly.
why: 〜わけではない is partial denial: not necessarily. 必ずしも and 〜からといって are near-certain signals for it.
〜わけがない is total denial ('no way'). 必ずしも cannot pair with a total denial.
〜ものか is an angry, spoken total denial. Same problem as わけがない, and the register is wrong too.
〜どころではない means 'far from that' or 'no room for it'. Neither pairs with 必ずしも, which needs a partial denial.
tell: 必ずしも or 〜からといって: partial denial, わけではない (or とは限らない).

s: 料理は好きだが、必ずしも毎日自分で作っている（　　）。忙しい日はコンビニの弁当で済ませることもある。
en: I like cooking, but I don't necessarily make my own meals every day. On busy days I sometimes make do with a convenience-store bento.
why: 〜わけではない is partial denial: not every day. 必ずしも must end in a partial denial, and 'sometimes a bento' shows it is only partly true.
〜わけがない is total denial ('no way'). 必ずしも ('not necessarily') cannot pair with a total denial.
〜わけだ means 'so it follows', an affirmative. 必ずしも needs a negative ending, and the next sentence says you don't cook every day.
〜わけにはいかない means 'I can't very well' for social reasons. 必ずしも does not pair with it, and nothing social is stopping you.
tell: 必ずしも + an 'all' word (毎日, いつも) partly denied: わけではない, never わけがない.

s: 今回の値上げは品質を守るための判断であり、決して利益を増やすことを目的としている（　　）。
en: This price rise was a decision made to protect quality. It is by no means aimed at increasing our profits.
c: わけではございません
わけにはまいりません
というものではございません
why: 〜わけではございません politely denies a reading someone might take (that it is about profit). 決して〜わけではない is a set pairing.
〜わけでございます is the polite 〜わけだ ('that is why'), an affirmative. 決して must be followed by a negative, so it cannot end this sentence.
〜わけにはまいりません means 'we cannot very well do it' for social reasons. The company is not refusing an action.
〜というものではない denies a rule of thumb (doing X alone is not enough). Nobody is claiming such a rule here.
cue: 品質を守るための判断であり
tell: 決して + 〜わけではない: politely correcting a wrong reading of your motive.

s: ただ長い時間机に向かっていれば成績が上がる（　　）。大切なのは勉強の中身だ。
en: Just sitting at a desk for long hours doesn't automatically raise your grades. What matters is what you actually study.
why: 〜ば + というものではない: meeting one condition (long hours) does not automatically give the result. It denies a rule of thumb.
〜どころではない means 'in no position to' (no time or room for it). Nothing is crowding out the grades.
〜わけにはいかない means 'I can't very well' for social reasons. Grades going up is not a social act.
〜わけだ means 'so it follows'. It would agree with the rule, but the next sentence rejects it.
cue: 大切なのは勉強の中身だ
tell: ただ〜ば + a result: というものではない. One condition alone is not enough.

s: 部下を育てるには、ただ厳しく叱れば（　　）。一人一人に合った指導が必要だ。
en: To develop your staff, it's not enough just to scold them hard. Each person needs guidance that suits them.
c: いいというものではない
why: 〜ばいいというものではない: one method alone does not guarantee the result. The next sentence gives what is really needed.
〜に違いない says the speaker is sure it is true. That would back harsh scolding, but the next sentence rejects it.
〜わけだ means 'so it follows'. It agrees that scolding is enough, which the next sentence denies.
〜どころではない means 'in no position to' or 'far beyond that level'. Neither meaning fits 'scolding is fine'.
cue: 一人一人に合った指導が必要だ
tell: ただ〜ばいい, then 'not so': いいというものではない.

s: 「フードロス」（　　）、まだ食べられるのに捨てられてしまう食品のことである。
en: 'Food loss' refers to food that gets thrown away even though it could still be eaten.
why: 〜とは defines a word. The frame 「X」とは、〜のことである is fixed, and common in reading passages.
〜となると needs a change in someone's behaviour, or a judgement about a real prospect. Nothing like that follows.
〜といったら stresses an extreme degree ('the X was something else'). A definition is not a degree.
〜といえば hops from a word to a related story ('speaking of'). It does not define anything.
tell: Term in 「」 + 〜のことである／〜という意味だ: とは.

s: 「ワーク・ライフ・バランス」とは、仕事と生活のどちらか一方を犠牲にせず、両方を（　　）。
en: 'Work-life balance' means making both work and private life fulfilling without sacrificing either one.
c: 充実させることである
充実させるわけがない
充実させるどころではない
why: 〜とは opens a definition, so the sentence must close like one: 〜ことである or 〜という意味だ.
〜わけがない is a total denial ('no way'). A definition does not end with a denial.
〜ものか is a heated spoken denial. It clashes with a written definition.
〜どころではない means 'in no position to'. It does not complete a definition.
cue: 「ワーク・ライフ・バランス」とは
tell: 「X」とは opens a definition: close it with 〜ことである.

s: A「来月、沖縄に出張することになったんです。」B「沖縄（　　）、先週うちの姉も旅行で行ってきましたよ。」
en: A: 'I'm going on a business trip to Okinawa next month.' B: 'Speaking of Okinawa, my sister went there on holiday just last week.'
why: 〜といえば picks up a word the other person just said (沖縄) and hops to your own related story.
〜とは defines a word or states its essence. B is not defining Okinawa.
〜となると needs someone's behaviour to change, or a judgement about a real prospect. B is just telling a story.
〜といっても says 'I say X, but it's less than it sounds'. B is not shrinking anything.
tell: Pick up the word just said and hop to a related story: といえば (speaking of).

s: 部長「来週の会議の準備は進んでる？」部下「はい。会議（　　）、会議室のプロジェクターがまだ修理中だそうです。」
en: Manager: 'How are preparations for next week's meeting going?' Staff: 'Fine. Speaking of the meeting, apparently the projector in the meeting room is still being repaired.'
why: 〜といえば picks up 会議 from the manager's question and moves on to a related point (the projector).
〜といっても lowers the image of X ('I say meeting, but it's only a small one'). Nothing is being played down.
〜とは defines a word. The staff member is not defining 'meeting'.
〜にしても means 'even if' or 'even granting X'. There is no concession here, just a related piece of news.
cue: プロジェクターがまだ修理中
tell: Take the word just said and add related news: といえば.

s: この部屋は駅から遠い（　　）遠いが、その分家賃が安くて静かだ。
en: This apartment is far from the station, I suppose, but in exchange the rent is cheap and it's quiet.
why: X といえば X が: grant the point for a moment, then say what really matters. The same word on both sides (遠い…遠い) is the giveaway.
〜となると needs a noun and a change in behaviour, or a real prospect. 遠いとなると遠い is not Japanese.
〜どころか means 'far from X'. 遠いどころか遠い contradicts itself.
〜とは defines a word. 遠いとは遠いが is not a pattern.
tell: Same word on both sides of the blank (遠い…遠いが): といえば. Grant it, then the real point.

s: A「新しく入った田中さん、仕事が遅いって聞いたけど、どう？」B「（　　）、その分ミスがほとんどないから助かっているよ。」
en: A: 'I heard the new guy, Tanaka, is slow at his work. How is he?' B: 'Slow, I suppose, yes, but he makes hardly any mistakes to make up for it, so he's a real help.'
c: 遅いといえば遅いけど
遅いどころか速いけど
why: X といえば X けど grants the point (yes, he is slow), then gives the real one. その分 ('to make up for it') confirms he is slow.
遅いどころか速い says he is actually fast. Then その分 has nothing to make up for.
遅いわけがない denies he is slow at all. その分 needs the slowness to be true.
〜にもかかわらず is stiff and needs a surprising result. 'Slow, and in exchange few mistakes' is a trade-off, not a surprise.
cue: 仕事が遅いって聞いた
tell: Concede by repeating the word (遅いといえば遅い), then the trade-off: といえば〜けど.

s: この町の名物（　　）、何と言っても川で取れる魚の塩焼きだ。
en: When you think of this town's local speciality, it has to be salt-grilled fish from the river.
why: 〜といえば names what springs to mind first from X. 何と言っても ('above all') is a typical follow-up.
〜といっても lowers the image of X ('I say speciality, but it's nothing much'). 何と言っても does the opposite.
〜にしても means 'even if' or 'even granting X'. There is nothing to concede here.
〜はともかく sets X aside to talk about something else. But the sentence goes on to name the speciality itself.
tell: X + what springs to mind first (何と言っても, やはり, まず): といえば／というと.

s: 子どものころの夏休み（　　）、近所の友達と毎日のように虫を捕りに行ったことを思い出す。
en: When I think of my childhood summer holidays, I remember going out to catch insects with the neighbourhood kids almost every day.
why: 〜というと brings up the memory or image linked to X. 〜を思い出す is a natural follow-up.
〜とは needs a definition ending (〜のことだ). This sentence ends with a memory, not a definition.
〜といっても lowers the image of X ('I say summer holiday, but it was short'). Nothing is being played down.
〜にしても means 'even if' or 'even granting X'. A memory is not a concession.
tell: X + a memory or image that comes to mind (思い出す, 思い浮かぶ): というと／といえば.

s: 普段はおとなしい兄だが、サッカーの話（　　）、急に声が大きくなって止まらなくなる。
en: My older brother is usually quiet, but once the talk turns to football, his voice suddenly gets loud and he won't stop.
why: 〜となると: when topic X comes up, the person turns into someone else. A visible change in behaviour must follow, and it does.
〜とは defines a word. Nothing here is being defined.
〜といっても lowers the image of X ('I say football talk, but...'). Nothing is being played down.
〜からといって needs 普通形 with だ (サッカーの話だからといって) and a 'doesn't mean' ending such as 〜とは限らない.
cue: 急に声が大きくなって
tell: Usually calm, but topic X sets them off: (のこと)となると.

s: 料理はほとんどしない夫だが、カレー（　　）、スパイスを何種類も買いそろえて一から作る。
en: My husband hardly ever cooks, but when it comes to curry, he buys in a whole range of spices and makes it from scratch.
why: 名 + のこととなると: when that subject comes up, the person behaves unlike their usual self. A husband who hardly cooks suddenly goes all out.
〜とは defines a word. カレーのこととは would need a definition ending (〜のことだ).
〜といっても lowers the image of X ('I say curry, but it's nothing much'). Here his effort goes up, not down.
〜はともかく sets X aside to talk about something else. But curry is exactly what he goes all out for.
tell: Usually one way, but topic X switches them into someone else: のこととなると.

s: 初めてオーロラを見たときの感動（　　）、今でも言葉では言い表せないほどだ。
en: The emotion I felt seeing the aurora for the first time was something else. Even now it's beyond words.
why: 〜といったら stresses that the degree was far beyond normal. It takes an abstract noun (感動, 驚き) and an 'indescribable' ending.
〜というと brings an image to mind or checks meaning. It does not stress a degree.
〜とは defines a word. 〜ほどだ states a degree, not a definition.
〜となると needs a change in someone's behaviour when a topic comes up. Nothing changes here.
cue: 言葉では言い表せない
tell: Abstract noun (感動, 驚き, 寒さ) + 'beyond words': といったら.

s: 大学の合格発表で自分の番号を見つけたときのうれしさ（　　）、思わずその場で母に電話してしまったほどだ。
en: The joy when I found my number on the university results board was something else: I phoned my mother on the spot without thinking.
why: 〜といったら stresses an extreme degree of a feeling (うれしさ). 〜ほどだ shows how extreme.
〜というと brings an image or memory to mind. It does not measure how strong a feeling was.
〜といっても lowers the image of X ('I say joy, but...'). The sentence raises it instead.
〜とは defines a word. 〜ほどだ states a degree, not a definition.
tell: Feeling noun + 〜ほどだ (so much that...): といったら.

s: 足をけがしていた（　　）、彼は最後まで試合に出続けた。
en: Even though he had injured his leg, he kept playing until the end of the match.
why: 〜にもかかわらず: an actual fact (the injury) failed to stop the result, which is surprising. A formal 〜のに.
〜からといって needs a 'doesn't mean' ending such as 〜とは限らない or 〜わけではない. Here a plain report of what he did follows.
〜を問わず also means 'regardless of' and needs a range noun. It cannot take a clause like けがしていた.
〜をめぐって means 'over' a dispute. Nobody is arguing.
cue: 最後まで試合に出続けた
tell: A real fact that should have stopped it, and didn't: にもかかわらず (a formal のに).

s: 平日の昼間（　　）、新しくできた美術館の前には長い行列ができていた。
en: Even though it was a weekday afternoon, there was a long queue outside the newly opened art museum.
why: 名 + にもかかわらず: a weekday afternoon should mean few visitors, yet there was a queue. It attaches straight to a noun and carries surprise.
〜を問わず means 'regardless of' and needs a range or a pair (平日・休日を問わず). 平日の昼間 is one setting, and the queue is a surprise, not a rule.
〜もかまわず criticises someone for ignoring what they should mind. A queue forming is not careless behaviour.
〜はさておき drops a topic to move to the main one. The sentence reports a surprise, not a change of topic.
cue: 長い行列ができていた
tell: A fact (平日の昼間) that should have meant the opposite + a surprising result: にもかかわらず.

s: 十分な証拠がある（　　）、警察はなぜか容疑者を逮捕しようとしない。
en: Even though there is enough evidence, for some reason the police are not trying to arrest the suspect.
why: 〜にもかかわらず: a fact (the evidence) should lead to an arrest, and it hasn't. なぜか marks the surprise.
〜からには ('now that ~') must be followed by resolve or duty (逮捕すべきだ). A puzzling non-action with なぜか cannot follow it.
〜といっても lowers the image of X ('I say there's evidence, but it's weak'). The second half does not shrink the evidence.
〜からといって denies an obvious conclusion and is followed by 〜とは限らない or 〜わけではない. Here an actual, puzzling situation follows.
tell: Fact + なぜか + the expected thing didn't happen: にもかかわらず (surprise).

s: 新しいパソコンを買った（　　）、忙しくてまだ一度も電源を入れていない。
en: I bought a new computer, and yet I've been so busy I haven't switched it on even once.
why: 〜ものの: X is a fact, but what you would expect from it did not happen. You buy a PC to use it, and it is still unused.
〜ものだから gives an excuse ('it's just that I bought one'). Buying a PC is no reason for not switching it on.
〜ものか is an angry denial at the end of a sentence. It cannot link two clauses.
〜ものなら means 'if only I could' and needs a potential verb in 辞書形 and a wish after it.
cue: まだ一度も電源を入れていない
tell: Did X, but the expected next step never happened (まだ〜ていない): ものの.

s: このアプリは便利な（　　）、操作が少し複雑なため、高齢の利用者からは不満の声も聞かれる。
en: This app is convenient, but because it is a little complicated to use, some older users have complained.
why: ナ形 + な + ものの: granted it is convenient, there is still a problem. 便利なものの is the correct connection.
〜にもかかわらず takes ナ形 + である (便利であるにもかかわらず). 便利なにもかかわらず is a connection error.
〜からといって takes 普通形 with だ (便利だからといって) and needs a 'doesn't mean' ending.
〜ものだから gives a reason or excuse. Being convenient does not cause the complaints.
tell: ナ形 + な + ものの. にもかかわらず needs である, からといって needs だ.

s: 新しいダイエット方法を三か月続けてみたものの、（　　）。
en: I kept up the new diet for three months, but my weight barely changed.
c: 体重はほとんど変わらなかった
体重が五キロも減った
みなさんもぜひ試してください
体重が減ったに違いない
why: After 〜ものの comes a result that goes against what the first fact leads you to expect. You diet to lose weight, and it barely moved.
Losing five kilos is exactly what you would expect from a diet. ものの needs a result that goes against that.
〜ものの bans requests and urging after it. 〜てください cannot follow.
〜に違いない is a guess. You would know your own weight, and the guess does not go against the first fact.
tell: 〜たものの → the expected result did NOT come. No requests after it.

s: この店は小さい（　　）、地元の人々に長く愛されている名店だ。
en: Small though it is, this shop is a well-known place that local people have loved for years.
why: State word + ながらも = 'although'. The subject is the same on both sides (the shop), and it admits a minus point first.
〜からといって needs a 'doesn't mean' ending (〜とは限らない). The sentence ends with a plain statement.
〜どころか would mean 'far from small', which denies that it is small at all.
〜ものなら needs a potential verb and a wish after it. It cannot attach to an adjective.
tell: State word (小さい, 狭い, 若い) + same subject + 'but': ながらも.

s: 地元の祭りを盛り上げるために、（　　）私にも何かお手伝いさせてください。
en: Please let me help in some way to make the local festival a success, small as my contribution may be.
why: 微力ながら is a humble set phrase: 'though my strength is small'. Noun + ながら admits a minus point, and a request may follow.
〜にもかかわらず bans requests after it. お手伝いさせてください is a request.
〜といっても lowers the image of X. 微力 is already modest, so there is nothing to lower.
〜からといって needs a 'doesn't mean' ending (〜わけではない). A request does not fit.
cue: お手伝いさせてください
tell: Humble opener before an offer to help: 微力ながら. Noun + ながら = although.

s: 夜中にラーメンを食べるのは体に悪いと（　　）、ついコンビニに寄ってしまう。
en: I know eating ramen in the middle of the night is bad for me, yet I still end up stopping at the convenience store.
why: Mind verb (わかる, 思う, 知る) + つつも: I know better, and I do it anyway. つい〜てしまう confirms the guilty habit.
〜たとたん is one sudden moment ('the instant I realised'). This is a repeated habit, not one moment.
〜次第 means 'as soon as' and needs a deliberate action after it. つい〜てしまう is the opposite of deliberate.
〜つつある means a change is in progress and ends a clause. It cannot mean 'although'.
cue: ついコンビニに寄ってしまう
tell: Mind verb + つつも + つい〜てしまう: knew better, did it anyway.

s: 健康のために毎朝走ろうと思いつつも、（　　）。
en: I keep meaning to go running every morning for my health, yet I end up oversleeping.
c: きっと誰かが起こしてくれるだろう
why: 〜つつも is followed by what you actually do, against what you meant to do. つい〜てしまう is the classic follow-up.
〜つつも needs a contrast: what you actually did against what you meant. 明日こそ必ず走ろう is just the same intention again, so there is no contrast.
〜つつも bans urging and invitations after it. 〜ましょう cannot follow.
〜つつも needs the same subject on both sides: I meant to run, and I did something else. 誰かが changes the subject.
tell: After 〜と思いつつも comes what you actually did against your intention, often つい〜てしまう.

s: 庭がある（　　）、テーブルが一つ置ける程度の小さなものです。
en: I say we have a garden, but it's just a small one with room for a single table.
why: 〜といっても: the real thing is smaller than the word suggests. You shrink the listener's picture of 'a garden'.
〜にもかかわらず needs a surprising result. 'We have a garden, and it is small' is not a surprise.
〜からといって denies an obvious conclusion and needs 〜とは限らない or 〜わけではない after it.
〜ばかりに needs a regrettable result caused by X. Having a garden does not cause it to be small.
tell: Say X, then shrink it (〜程度, 〜だけ): といっても.

s: A「連休はどこかへ行きましたか。」B「ええ、旅行に行った（　　）、近くの温泉に一泊しただけですけどね。」
en: A: 'Did you go anywhere over the long weekend?' B: 'Yes, I went on a trip. Though really it was just one night at a nearby hot spring.'
why: 〜といっても corrects the picture downward: 'a trip' sounds big, but it was one night nearby. 〜だけ confirms it.
〜にもかかわらず needs a surprising result, and it is stiff for casual chat. One night away is not a surprise.
〜からといって needs a 'doesn't mean' ending (〜とは限らない). B simply describes the trip.
〜どころか says reality is far beyond or opposite to X. B is shrinking X, not denying it.
tell: 'I did X, though it was only...' (〜だけ, 〜程度): といっても.

s: 有名な大学を出た（　　）、仕事ができるとは限らない。
en: Just because someone graduated from a famous university doesn't necessarily mean they're good at their job.
why: 〜からといって: the reason X alone is not enough for the usual conclusion. 〜とは限らない after it is the matching pair.
〜ことだし gives a light reason and needs an intention or invitation after it (〜しよう).
〜にもかかわらず needs an actual, surprising result, not a general 'not necessarily'.
〜ばかりに means one cause led to a regrettable result. 〜とは限らない is not a result.
tell: 〜とは限らない／〜わけではない at the end: からといって at the start.

s: 模試で合格点が取れた（　　）、油断してはいけません。本番まではまだ一か月あります。
en: Just because you got a pass mark on the mock exam doesn't mean you can relax. There's still a month until the real exam.
why: 〜からといって + 〜てはいけない: X does not justify the obvious next step (relaxing). A warning can follow からといって.
〜にもかかわらず bans urging and warnings after it. 〜てはいけません cannot follow.
〜おかげで credits X for a good result and bans urging or warnings after it.
〜ばかりに needs a regrettable result caused by X. A warning is not a result.
cue: 油断してはいけません
tell: Just because X, don't do Y (〜てはいけない): からといって. にもかかわらず refuses warnings.

s: 一度上司に注意されたからといって、（　　）。
en: Just because your boss told you off once, there's no need to get so down about it.
c: そんなに落ち込むことはない
落ち込まずにはいられない
why: 〜からといって is followed by a denial of the obvious conclusion. 〜ことはない (there's no need to) does that.
〜に違いない agrees with the obvious conclusion (you'll be down). からといって needs the opposite.
〜ずにはいられない (can't help it) also agrees with the obvious conclusion.
〜わけだ (so it follows) agrees with it too. からといって rejects it.
tell: からといって needs a 'no' after it: 〜ことはない, 〜わけではない, 〜とは限らない.

s: もし宝くじで一億円が（　　）、まず何に使いますか。
en: If you won 100 million yen in the lottery, what would you spend it on first?
why: 〜としたら is pure supposition and pairs with もし. A question about what you would do can follow.
〜からには means 'now that' and needs a real, settled fact. もし rules that out.
〜ものなら needs a potential verb and a wish (〜たい) after it, not a question.
〜ないことには means 'unless' and needs a negative result after it.
tell: もし + pure supposition + a question or judgement: としたら.

s: もし今の仕事を辞めて好きなことができる（　　）、田舎で小さなパン屋を開きたい。
en: If I could quit my job and do whatever I liked, I'd want to open a small bakery in the countryside.
why: 〜としたら is pure supposition and pairs with もし. A wish (〜たい) can follow it.
〜からには ('now that ~') needs a settled fact. もし marks a daydream, so からには cannot follow it.
〜にもかかわらず needs a fact that has actually happened. もし marks a supposition, so the two clash.
〜ばかりに needs a real cause and a regretted result that already happened. A daydream and a wish are neither.
tell: もし + a supposition + a wish (〜たい): としたら. からには and にもかかわらず need a real fact.

s: 来月から本当に一人暮らしをするとなると、（　　）。
en: If I really am going to live on my own from next month, just getting the furniture together will cost quite a lot.
c: 家具をそろえるだけでもかなりお金がかかるだろう
ぜひ一人暮らしをしてみたい
ぜひ一人暮らしをしてください
家具はそろえずに済んだ
why: 〜となると looks at a real prospect and is followed by a judgement about it: here, what it will cost.
This just repeats the first half: you already plan to live alone, so 'I'd love to try it' adds nothing. となると needs a judgement about what the prospect involves.
It urges the very thing the first half already assumes will happen, so it says nothing. となると needs a judgement about what the prospect involves.
〜となると looks ahead at a prospect. A past result (済んだ) cannot follow.
tell: となると + a judgement about what the prospect will involve (〜だろう, 〜必要だ).

s: （　　）、もう一度大学一年生からやり直したい。
en: If I could do it over, I'd want to start again from my first year of university.
c: やり直さないことには
why: Potential verb + ものなら + a wish: if it were possible (and it isn't), I'd want to. Repeating the verb is natural.
〜(よ)うものなら warns that a disaster would follow. A wish (〜たい) is the wrong kind of ending.
〜ないことには needs a negative result after it ('unless I redo it, nothing works').
〜たところ reports what turned out after something you actually did. A wish about going back cannot follow it.
tell: 可能形 + ものなら + 〜たい: if only I could. Volitional + ものなら is the disaster version.

s: A「この問題、簡単すぎて小学生でも解けるよ。」B「へえ、そんなに言うなら、（　　）解いてみてよ。」
en: A: 'This problem is so easy even a primary school kid could solve it.' B: 'Oh really? If you're going to say that, go on, solve it if you can.'
why: Potential verb + ものなら + the same verb + てみろ／てみて is a dare: 'go on, do it if you can'.
〜(よ)うものなら warns that a disaster would follow. B is daring A, not warning.
〜ないことには means 'unless' and needs a negative result after it.
〜としても means 'even if', which clashes with a dare. 'Even if you can, try it' makes no sense.
tell: Potential verb + ものなら + the same verb + てみろ: a dare ('try it if you can').

s: うちの父は厳しくて、門限を一分でも（　　）、一週間は口をきいてくれない。
en: My dad is strict: if I'm even one minute past curfew, he won't speak to me for a week.
why: Volitional + ものなら: if you dared to do X, something awful would follow. 〜でも ('even just') often comes before it.
辞書形 + ものなら is the wistful 'if only I could'. It needs a potential verb and a wish after it.
〜ないことには would mean 'unless I'm late, he won't talk to me'. That logic is backwards.
〜どころか means 'far from X'. 'Far from passing curfew' makes no sense here.
tell: 〜でも + volitional + ものなら → a bad outcome: (よ)うものなら.

s: あの部長の前で会社の悪口を一言でも（　　）、ただでは済まないだろう。
en: If you said even one bad word about the company in front of that department head, you wouldn't get away with it.
why: Volitional + ものなら + a guess of disaster: 'if you so much as said it, there'd be trouble'. ただでは済まないだろう is that guess.
Potential + ものなら needs a wish or a dare after it ('if only I could say it'). A warning of trouble does not fit.
〜ないことには means 'unless'. 'Unless you speak ill of the company, you'll be in trouble' is backwards.
〜からといって needs a 'doesn't mean' ending (〜とは限らない). ただでは済まない is a prediction, not a denial.
cue: ただでは済まないだろう
tell: 一言でも + volitional + ものなら + 'there'd be trouble': (よ)うものなら.

s: 実際に（　　）、この機械が本当に便利かどうかはわからない。
en: Unless you actually try it out, you can't tell whether this machine is really convenient.
c: 使ってみないことには
使ってみようものなら
why: 〜ないことには: without doing X, nothing can be known or done. A negative (わからない) must follow, and it does.
〜てはじめて means 'only after X did I realise' and needs a positive realisation after it (わかった). It clashes with わからない.
〜ものなら needs a potential verb and a wish after it.
〜(よ)うものなら needs a disaster after it. 'I can't tell' is not a disaster.
tell: Not until you do X + a negative (わからない, 何とも言えない): ないことには.

s: どんなに好きな仕事でも、体が健康で（　　）、長く続けることはできない。
en: However much you love your job, you can't keep it up for long unless you're physically healthy.
why: ナ形 + で + ないことには: unless the condition is met, it can't happen. A negative (できない) follows.
〜からといって needs a 'doesn't mean' ending. 'Just because you're healthy, you can't keep working' makes no sense.
〜ものの means 'X is true, but'. 'You're healthy, but you can't keep working' turns the point of the sentence upside down.
〜(よ)うものなら warns of a disaster that would follow an act. Being healthy is not a risky act.
cue: 続けることはできない
tell: でない + ことには + a negative (できない): unless X, it won't happen.

s: 詳しいお見積もりにつきましては、一度現場を（　　）。
en: As for a detailed quote, we are unable to provide one until we have seen the site.
c: 拝見しないことには、お出しできかねます
拝見しないことには、すぐにお出しします
拝見したところ、お出しできかねます
拝見しようものなら、お出しできかねます
why: 〜ないことには + a polite negative (〜かねます): until we see the site, we cannot quote. Business keigo throughout.
〜ないことには must be followed by a negative. すぐにお出しします is positive.
〜たところ reports what happened after something you already did. The site visit has not happened yet (一度 looks ahead).
〜(よ)うものなら warns of a disaster after a risky act. Visiting the site is the normal next step, not a risk.
tell: Polite 'not until we've seen it': 〜ないことには + 〜かねます (a negative).

s: 多くのボランティアの支え（　　）、今回のマラソン大会の成功はありえなかった。
en: Without the support of so many volunteers, this marathon could never have succeeded.
why: 〜を抜きにしては: without X (something the speaker values), the result could not happen. A negative (ありえなかった) follows.
〜に応じて means adjusting to match a variable. Nothing is being adjusted.
〜を問わず means 'regardless of', which would say the volunteers didn't matter. That is the opposite meaning.
〜をもとに means using X as material to make something. Success is not made out of support as material.
tell: A valued X + 'could not have happened': を抜きにしては.

s: この町の経済は、江戸時代から続く酒造り（　　）成り立たない。
en: This town's economy could not survive without sake brewing, which has continued since the Edo period.
why: 〜を抜きにしては: without X, the thing cannot stand. A negative (成り立たない) follows, and X is something the speaker values.
〜にかかわらず means 'regardless of', which would say sake brewing doesn't matter. That clashes with the point.
〜はさておき drops a topic to move to the main one. But sake brewing is the main point here.
〜を通じて means 'through' a go-between. 'Cannot stand through sake brewing' makes no sense.
tell: Without (valued) X + cannot (成り立たない, 語れない): を抜きにしては.

s: たとえ今から急いで空港に向かった（　　）、最終便には間に合わないだろう。
en: Even if we headed for the airport right now, we probably wouldn't make the last flight.
why: 〜としても: even supposing X, the outcome does not change. It must be hypothetical, and たとえ is the signal.
〜ものの needs a fact that has already happened. たとえ marks a supposition.
〜からには means 'now that' and needs a real fact, then resolve or duty. たとえ rules out a real fact.
〜ばかりに needs a real cause and a regretted result that already happened. たとえ makes this a supposition.
tell: たとえ + a supposition: としても.

s: 確かに昨日は雨だった（　　）、あそこまで客が少ないとは思わなかった。
en: Granted it was raining yesterday, I still never thought there would be that few customers.
why: 〜にしても can take a known fact: 'granted X, still...'. 確かに shows the rain really happened, and 〜とは思わなかった is the 'still'.
〜としたら sets up a supposition and needs a conclusion drawn from it. 確かに states a known fact, and 'I never thought it would be that quiet' is not a conclusion from rain.
〜にもかかわらず says the result defied the fact. But rain would explain few customers, not defy it.
〜ばかりに must lead straight to the bad result it caused. Here 〜とは思わなかった follows, which is the speaker's surprise, not the result.
tell: 確かに + a known fact, then 'still...': にしても. としたら only supposes and draws a conclusion.

s: どの大学に（　　）、入学後に何を学びたいのかをはっきりさせておくべきだ。
en: Whichever university you go to, you should be clear about what you want to study once you're there.
why: Question word + にせよ: whichever it is, the judgement holds. 〜べきだ (a judgement) follows naturally.
〜(よ)うものなら warns of a disaster. 'You should be clear about your goals' is advice, not a disaster.
